case_info.scenario: A man in his 60s with anti-RNA polymerase 3–positive diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (dcSSc) diagnosed 1 year prior, presented with a 6-month history of lesions on the abdomen. Physical examination demonstrated red-brown, ovoid, smooth hypertrophic plaques on the upper and lower abdomen (Figure 1A), in addition to confluent sclerosis involving the bilateral fingers and hands with proximal extension to involve the upper extremities. The abdominal lesions were asymptomatic, and he had not applied any topical treatments to the affected skin. He denied any preceding trauma or acne. Despite ongoing treatment with oral mycophenolate sodium, 720 mg, twice daily, and subcutaneous tocilizumab, 162 mg, weekly, his cutaneous sclerosis had continued to progress. A punch biopsy of an abdominal plaque was obtained to guide the diagnosis and management of the new lesions (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Red-brown plaques without secondary change were scattered on the chest and abdomen. White patches with focally retained follicular pigment were also noted on the trunk. B, A square biopsy reveals thickened collagen bundles, increased spindle cells, loss of follicular units, and superficial displacement of eccrine glands with absent perieccrine adiposity.
case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated a square-shaped biopsy specimen with an unremarkable epidermis. An increased population of interstitial spindle cells in the superficial dermis was noted, which decreased in density as the collagen bundles became more noticeably thickened in a descending pattern (Figure 2). There was also superficial displacement of eccrine glands with loss of perieccrine fat. A significant inflammatory infiltrate was absent, but rare perieccrine plasma cells were identified. Verhoeff–Van Gieson stain showed a normal density of elastic fibers. CD34 demonstrated complete loss of dermal dendritic cells within the spindled infiltrate. SMA showed focal and patchy expression. Based on the clinical presentation and histological findings, nodular (keloidal) morphea in the setting of dcSSC was diagnosed. The patient was continued on his systemic immunomodulatory treatment with mycophenolate and tocilizumab. He was recommended to initiate UVA-1 phototherapy, but due to issues with insurance coverage, he was unable to do so. The patient started a topical regimen alternating calcipotriene, 0.005%, cream and clobetasol, 0.05%, to the hands, which stabilized sclerosis progression at this site. Treatment was deferred for the abdominal plaques given the asymptomatic nature. Nodular morphea is a rare variant of localized scleroderma, first described by Thomas Addison in the 1800s as an “untrue keloid.”1It presents as firm, indurated plaques or nodules, often mimicking granulomatous, inflammatory, and neoplastic cutaneous conditions, such as sarcoidosis, hypertrophic scars and keloids, and smooth muscle tumors.2Although the origin of nodular morphea remains unknown, the pathogenesis is related to excessive fibroblast activation and collagen deposition.3The classification of nodular morphea as a distinct entity remains debated. While some consider it a variant of localized scleroderma, many case reports involve patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc), often with concurrent visceral involvement.4Similar to this patient, the lesions associated with nodular morphea typically appear within the first 6 months following a diagnosis of SSc, during the active disease phase.5,6However, in some instances, nodular morphea may precede other signs and symptoms of SSc, and may potentially serve as a harbinger of systemic disease.6 Given the nonspecific presentation of nodular morphea, thorough clinical history and histopathology are critical for accurate diagnosis. Nodular morphea often resembles hypertrophic scar both clinically and histologically, making accurate diagnosis challenging. Clinically, a history of trauma should be present in hypertrophic scar and absent in morphea. However, nodular morphea may closely mimic a hypertrophic scar due to nodular fibrosis and increased cellularity that is not typically observed in other variants of morphea.3On immunohistochemistry, while hypertrophic scars may also demonstrate loss of CD34 and focal SMA expression, they also demonstrate elastolysis, which was not present in this patient’s results. In this patient, the biopsy revealed diminished adnexal structures, superficial displacement of eccrine glands with perieccrine fat pad loss, and hypercellularity more prominent in the upper dermis. While there was not a significant lymphocytic infiltrate, the overall findings and history support the diagnosis of nodular morphea as opposed to hypertrophic scar.7 Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma presents with multiple cutaneous leiomyomas (CLMs), which typically appear as smooth pink papules and plaques that may resemble nodular morphea. However, CLMs are characteristically painful and may occur concurrently with uterine leiomyomas and renal cell carcinoma.8Histopathologic examination of CLMs additionally revealed disorganized clusters of smooth muscle cells with positive immunohistochemical staining for smooth muscle markers. While dermatomyofibroma and nodular morphea may have overlapping clinical and histological features, dermatomyofibroma usually spares the adnexal structures. In this patient, the spindle cells and thickened collagen have replaced normal follicular units.9,10 Treatment is not standardized owing to the rarity of nodular morphea. Topical corticosteroids and immunomodulators are often used, and UVA-1 phototherapy may be beneficial in some patients.2In this patient, additional treatments were deferred as he was asymptomatic, already on systemic therapy for dcSSc, and UVA-1 phototherapy was not feasible. Further research is needed to clarify the pathogenesis and optimal management strategy of nodular morphea, both in patients with and without underlying SSc. Distinguishing this entity from its clinical mimickers is essential to reduce unnecessary interventions and initiate effective treatments.

case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated a square-shaped biopsy specimen with an unremarkable epidermis. An increased population of interstitial spindle cells in the superficial dermis was noted, which decreased in density as the collagen bundles became more noticeably thickened in a descending pattern (Figure 2). There was also superficial displacement of eccrine glands with loss of perieccrine fat. A significant inflammatory infiltrate was absent, but rare perieccrine plasma cells were identified. Verhoeff–Van Gieson stain showed a normal density of elastic fibers. CD34 demonstrated complete loss of dermal dendritic cells within the spindled infiltrate. SMA showed focal and patchy expression. Based on the clinical presentation and histological findings, nodular (keloidal) morphea in the setting of dcSSC was diagnosed. The patient was continued on his systemic immunomodulatory treatment with mycophenolate and tocilizumab. He was recommended to initiate UVA-1 phototherapy, but due to issues with insurance coverage, he was unable to do so. The patient started a topical regimen alternating calcipotriene, 0.005%, cream and clobetasol, 0.05%, to the hands, which stabilized sclerosis progression at this site. Treatment was deferred for the abdominal plaques given the asymptomatic nature. Nodular morphea is a rare variant of localized scleroderma, first described by Thomas Addison in the 1800s as an “untrue keloid.”1It presents as firm, indurated plaques or nodules, often mimicking granulomatous, inflammatory, and neoplastic cutaneous conditions, such as sarcoidosis, hypertrophic scars and keloids, and smooth muscle tumors.2Although the origin of nodular morphea remains unknown, the pathogenesis is related to excessive fibroblast activation and collagen deposition.3The classification of nodular morphea as a distinct entity remains debated. While some consider it a variant of localized scleroderma, many case reports involve patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc), often with concurrent visceral involvement.4Similar to this patient, the lesions associated with nodular morphea typically appear within the first 6 months following a diagnosis of SSc, during the active disease phase.5,6However, in some instances, nodular morphea may precede other signs and symptoms of SSc, and may potentially serve as a harbinger of systemic disease.6 Given the nonspecific presentation of nodular morphea, thorough clinical history and histopathology are critical for accurate diagnosis. Nodular morphea often resembles hypertrophic scar both clinically and histologically, making accurate diagnosis challenging. Clinically, a history of trauma should be present in hypertrophic scar and absent in morphea. However, nodular morphea may closely mimic a hypertrophic scar due to nodular fibrosis and increased cellularity that is not typically observed in other variants of morphea.3On immunohistochemistry, while hypertrophic scars may also demonstrate loss of CD34 and focal SMA expression, they also demonstrate elastolysis, which was not present in this patient’s results. In this patient, the biopsy revealed diminished adnexal structures, superficial displacement of eccrine glands with perieccrine fat pad loss, and hypercellularity more prominent in the upper dermis. While there was not a significant lymphocytic infiltrate, the overall findings and history support the diagnosis of nodular morphea as opposed to hypertrophic scar.7 Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma presents with multiple cutaneous leiomyomas (CLMs), which typically appear as smooth pink papules and plaques that may resemble nodular morphea. However, CLMs are characteristically painful and may occur concurrently with uterine leiomyomas and renal cell carcinoma.8Histopathologic examination of CLMs additionally revealed disorganized clusters of smooth muscle cells with positive immunohistochemical staining for smooth muscle markers. While dermatomyofibroma and nodular morphea may have overlapping clinical and histological features, dermatomyofibroma usually spares the adnexal structures. In this patient, the spindle cells and thickened collagen have replaced normal follicular units.9,10 Treatment is not standardized owing to the rarity of nodular morphea. Topical corticosteroids and immunomodulators are often used, and UVA-1 phototherapy may be beneficial in some patients.2In this patient, additional treatments were deferred as he was asymptomatic, already on systemic therapy for dcSSc, and UVA-1 phototherapy was not feasible. Further research is needed to clarify the pathogenesis and optimal management strategy of nodular morphea, both in patients with and without underlying SSc. Distinguishing this entity from its clinical mimickers is essential to reduce unnecessary interventions and initiate effective treatments.

An increased population of interstitial spindle cells in the superficial dermis was noted, which decreased in density as the collagen bundles became more noticeably thickened in a descending pattern (Figure 2). There was also superficial displacement of eccrine glands with loss of perieccrine fat. A significant inflammatory infiltrate was absent, but rare perieccrine plasma cells were identified. Verhoeff–Van Gieson stain showed a normal density of elastic fibers. CD34 demonstrated complete loss of dermal dendritic cells within the spindled infiltrate. SMA showed focal and patchy expression. Based on the clinical presentation and histological findings, nodular (keloidal) morphea in the setting of dcSSC was diagnosed. The patient was continued on his systemic immunomodulatory treatment with mycophenolate and tocilizumab. He was recommended to initiate UVA-1 phototherapy, but due to issues with insurance coverage, he was unable to do so. The patient started a topical regimen alternating calcipotriene, 0.005%, cream and clobetasol, 0.05%, to the hands, which stabilized sclerosis progression at this site. Treatment was deferred for the abdominal plaques given the asymptomatic nature. Nodular morphea is a rare variant of localized scleroderma, first described by Thomas Addison in the 1800s as an “untrue keloid.”1It presents as firm, indurated plaques or nodules, often mimicking granulomatous, inflammatory, and neoplastic cutaneous conditions, such as sarcoidosis, hypertrophic scars and keloids, and smooth muscle tumors.2Although the origin of nodular morphea remains unknown, the pathogenesis is related to excessive fibroblast activation and collagen deposition.3The classification of nodular morphea as a distinct entity remains debated. While some consider it a variant of localized scleroderma, many case reports involve patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc), often with concurrent visceral involvement.4Similar to this patient, the lesions associated with nodular morphea typically appear within the first 6 months following a diagnosis of SSc, during the active disease phase.5,6However, in some instances, nodular morphea may precede other signs and symptoms of SSc, and may potentially serve as a harbinger of systemic disease.6 Given the nonspecific presentation of nodular morphea, thorough clinical history and histopathology are critical for accurate diagnosis. Nodular morphea often resembles hypertrophic scar both clinically and histologically, making accurate diagnosis challenging. Clinically, a history of trauma should be present in hypertrophic scar and absent in morphea. However, nodular morphea may closely mimic a hypertrophic scar due to nodular fibrosis and increased cellularity that is not typically observed in other variants of morphea.3On immunohistochemistry, while hypertrophic scars may also demonstrate loss of CD34 and focal SMA expression, they also demonstrate elastolysis, which was not present in this patient’s results. In this patient, the biopsy revealed diminished adnexal structures, superficial displacement of eccrine glands with perieccrine fat pad loss, and hypercellularity more prominent in the upper dermis. While there was not a significant lymphocytic infiltrate, the overall findings and history support the diagnosis of nodular morphea as opposed to hypertrophic scar.7 Hereditary leiomyomatosis and renal cell carcinoma presents with multiple cutaneous leiomyomas (CLMs), which typically appear as smooth pink papules and plaques that may resemble nodular morphea. However, CLMs are characteristically painful and may occur concurrently with uterine leiomyomas and renal cell carcinoma.8Histopathologic examination of CLMs additionally revealed disorganized clusters of smooth muscle cells with positive immunohistochemical staining for smooth muscle markers. While dermatomyofibroma and nodular morphea may have overlapping clinical and histological features, dermatomyofibroma usually spares the adnexal structures. In this patient, the spindle cells and thickened collagen have replaced normal follicular units.9,10 Treatment is not standardized owing to the rarity of nodular morphea. Topical corticosteroids and immunomodulators are often used, and UVA-1 phototherapy may be beneficial in some patients.2In this patient, additional treatments were deferred as he was asymptomatic, already on systemic therapy for dcSSc, and UVA-1 phototherapy was not feasible. Further research is needed to clarify the pathogenesis and optimal management strategy of nodular morphea, both in patients with and without underlying SSc. Distinguishing this entity from its clinical mimickers is essential to reduce unnecessary interventions and initiate effective treatments.

case_info.explanation: Histopathology demonstrated a square-shaped biopsy specimen with an unremarkable epidermis. An increased population of interstitial spindle cells in the superficial dermis was noted, which decreased in density as the collagen bundles became more noticeably thickened in a descending pattern (Figure 2). There was also superficial displacement of eccrine glands with loss of perieccrine fat. A significant inflammatory infiltrate was absent, but rare perieccrine plasma cells were identified. Verhoeff–Van Gieson stain showed a normal density of elastic fibers. CD34 demonstrated complete loss of dermal dendritic cells within the spindled infiltrate. SMA showed focal and patchy expression. Based on the clinical presentation and histological findings, nodular (keloidal) morphea in the setting of dcSSC was diagnosed. The patient was continued on his systemic immunomodulatory treatment with mycophenolate and tocilizumab. He was recommended to initiate UVA-1 phototherapy, but due to issues with insurance coverage, he was unable to do so. The patient started a topical regimen alternating calcipotriene, 0.005%, cream and clobetasol, 0.05%, to the hands, which stabilized sclerosis progression at this site. Treatment was deferred for the abdominal plaques given the asymptomatic nature. Nodular morphea is a rare variant of localized scleroderma, first described by Thomas Addison in the 1800s as an “untrue keloid.”1It presents as firm, indurated plaques or nodules, often mimicking granulomatous, inflammatory, and neoplastic cutaneous conditions, such as sarcoidosis, hypertrophic scars and keloids, and smooth muscle tumors.2Although the origin of nodular morphea remains unknown, the pathogenesis is related to excessive fibroblast activation and collagen deposition.3The classification of nodular morphea as a distinct entity remains debated.
